name: Spanish lessons
about: The path through the first Spanish words, a few at a time, each in everyday sentences written for its lesson. Word list: FrequencyWords by Hermit Dave, from OpenSubtitles (opensubtitles.org), CC BY-SA 4.0.

words.tomar: to drink, to have; to take
words.sí: yes; a reflexive pronoun after a preposition
words.estar: to be (where something is, how someone is)
words.conocer: to know, to be acquainted with
words.quedar: to stay, to remain; to fit or suit
words.esperar: to wait, to wait for; to hope
words.nada: nothing; anything in a negative sentence
words.nadie: nobody; anybody in a negative sentence
words.su: his, her, its, their, your formal
words.le: to him, to her, to you formally
words.se: himself, herself, itself, themselves; se before lo, la, los or las
words.lo: him; it, as a masculine singular direct object; the neuter article in lo mismo
words.agarrar: to take hold of, to grab
words.volver: to return, to come back, to go back
words.sacar: to take out, to get out
words.razón: reason; tener razón means to be right
words.tratar: to deal with; tratar de means to be about
words.casar: to marry; casarse means to get married
words.acompañar: to accompany, to come along with
words.cuenta: account; own initiative in por mi cuenta
words.revés: reverse side; the other way in al revés
words.lamentar: to regret, to be sorry about
words.caramba: darn; an exclamation of surprise or frustration
words.noticia: news item; news in the plural
words.echar: to throw, to put; to take a look in echar un vistazo
words.tierra: earth, land; Earth as the planet
words.partir: to depart, to split; a partir de means starting from
words.comunicar: to communicate; comunicarse con means to get in touch with

por-favor.about: Literally for favor: add it to any request.

como-estas.about: Literally how are you: to someone you say tú to.

un-momento.about: Use un momento for a short stretch of time.

perdon.about: Also used to get attention politely: excuse me.

concept.line: Every noun is masculine (el teléfono) or feminine (la mesa): learn which with the word. agua is feminine, though it takes el: el agua.
A question opens with ¿ and closes with ?. After a question word like dónde, the verb usually comes next: ¿Dónde está el carro?
The verb's ending already says who, so yo and tú are left out unless it matters who: Tomas café (you drink coffee), but Tú tomas café y yo tomo té.
mi (my) goes before the noun, the same for el and la words: mi libro, mi llave.
estar says where something is and how someone is: Está aquí, Estoy bien. ser says what something is and whose it is: Es un libro, Es de mi mamá.
no goes right before the verb: No tomo café, Ella no viene. Answering a question with no, the first no is the answer and the second goes before the verb: No, no tomo leche.

concept.line: After querer, the next verb stays in its basic form, the one ending in -ar, -er or -ir: Quiero comer (I want to eat), ¿Quieres tomar un café?
A verb's ending says who does it: tomo (I drink), tomas (you drink), toma (he or she drinks); como (I eat), comemos (we eat).

concept.line: The thing or activity liked controls gustar: Me gusta quedarme en casa. Use gusta with one thing or an infinitive activity, gustan with plural things. me or te says who likes it.

words.means: doy = I give; dame = give me, telling tú
hice = I did or made; hiciste = you did or made
trabajé = I worked; trabajaste = you worked
llamé = I called; llamó = he or she called

concept.line: The preterite presents an event as completed: Hoy trabajé en casa. Learn each person's form: hice, hiciste; trabajé, trabajaste. A completed event today can use this tense too.

lessons.title: What did you have for lunch?

words.means: he = I have; has = you have, before a participle
tomado = had or drunk; tomé = I had or drank
visto = seen; vi = I saw; verla = to watch it

concept.line: The present perfect uses haber plus an unchanged participle: he comido, has tomado. It can connect an event with the present. Compare Ayer comí en casa. The choice between these tenses varies by region and context; hoy does not require the perfect.

words.means: fui = I went; fuiste = you went
vine = I came; vino = he or she came
me quedé = I stayed; te quedaste = you stayed

concept.line: Irregular preterites include fui and fuiste from ir, and vine and vino from venir. quedarse keeps its pronoun: me quedé, te quedaste. The forms say who went, came or stayed.

words.means: escuchar = to listen to; escucho = I listen to
ha = he, she or you formally has, before a participle

concept.line: Learn the whole pattern: esperar a alguien, escuchar música, ayudar a alguien con algo, hablar con alguien. English for or to does not automatically need its own Spanish preposition. Personal a still marks a specific human object.

Descriptive adjectives usually follow the noun and agree with it: un lugar bonito, una casa bonita. Some adjectives can precede the noun with a different emphasis or meaning; that order is not automatically wrong.

words.means: se = the pronoun in se llama

words.means: llevar = to take; llevo = I take; llevarlo = to take it
lo = it, replacing a masculine singular object
preguntar = to ask; preguntarme = to ask me; preguntarle = to ask him, her or you formally
duele = hurts; duelen = hurt, with plural subjects

lessons.title: Asking someone to put a book here

words.means: agarra = take, telling tú; agarre = take, telling usted; agarren = take, telling ustedes

tirar = to throw; tira = throw, telling tú; no tires = do not throw, telling tú

concept.line: Use pon with tú, ponga with usted and pongan with ustedes. Negative tú commands use present-subjunctive forms: no tires. Object pronouns attach to affirmative commands and precede negative commands: dame, no lo pongas.

words.means: cerrar = to close; cierra = close, telling tú

los = the, with masculine plural nouns

concept.line: Common plurals add -s after a vowel and -es after many consonants: libro/libros, foto/fotos, ciudad/ciudades. Articles and describing words agree: los libros, las fotos, varias ciudades. Plural subjects take plural verbs.

words.means: uno, una = one, standing for a known noun
ninguno, ninguna = none, standing for a known noun

concept.line: A number can stand for a noun already named: ¿Necesitas libros? Tengo dos. Use uno for a masculine noun, una for a feminine noun. ninguno and ninguna mean none; after the verb, keep no: No tengo ninguno. Before a masculine singular noun, use un or ningún.

words.means: volver = to return; vuelvo = I return; volvimos = we returned

concept.line: An infinitive can name the action being described: Es seguro caminar aquí. Use para for the purpose in tiempo para comer. With a thing described as difficult to understand, use de: Esta palabra es difícil de entender. The construction decides the link; English to has no single Spanish equivalent.

lessons.title: Keeping in touch during a busy week

nos = us; with a plural subject, can mean each other

the way; de otra manera = in a different way

tienen = they have, or you all have

concept.line: Use subject pronouns when they identify a contrast: Ustedes van, nosotros no. A subject can stand alone when its verb is understood. Leave it out when the ending and context make it clear.

words.means: me siento = I feel; te sientes = you feel; se siente = he or she feels

concept.line: To describe how someone feels, sentirse uses a pronoun matching that person: me siento, te sientes, se siente. With a body part as the object, sentir can be used without that pronoun: No siento el brazo.

concept.line: A question can be part of another sentence: ¿Sabe dónde está mi carro? Keep the accent in dónde, qué, cómo, cuándo and por qué. For whether, use si without an accent: No sé si ella vive aquí.

words.means: mirar = to look at; mira = look, telling tú

concept.line: Por favor makes a request polite; un momento asks for a short amount of time. Match the command to the listener: espera for tú, espere for usted. These expressions soften the request without changing its command form.

concept.line: The simple future adds endings to the infinitive or an irregular stem: trabajaré, iré. It can make a prediction or promise. ir a plus an infinitive also refers to the future: Voy a llamar. The two forms often overlap.

words.means: olvido = I forget; olvidé = I forgot; olvidar = to forget
prometo = I promise; prometer = to promise

lessons.title: Supporting someone after losing a pet

words.means: cuidar = to take care of; cuido = I take care of; cuidas = you take care of
the part; de tu parte = of you
fue = he, she or it was, preterite
tuviera = had, in an imagined condition
haría = would do; harías = you would do

concept.line: The conditional expresses would and softens requests: me gustaría, ¿podrías?, sería. For an imagined condition, use si plus the imperfect subjunctive and a conditional result: Si tuviera tiempo, iría contigo. The condition is imagined, not a statement about past time.

words.means: elegir = to choose; elijo = I choose
where, linking a place to a description
leí = I read, in the past

concept.line: A relative clause describes a named person or thing: el libro que quiero, the book I want. Spanish keeps que even when English omits that. donde links a place to what happens there: la ciudad donde vivo. Relative que and donde have no written accent.

words.means: vivía = used to live, was living
estaba = was, for a past state or location

concept.line: The imperfect presents past habits, states or ongoing background: Antes vivía aquí. The preterite presents a bounded event: Cuando llegué, llovía. arrived gives the event; was raining gives its background. These tenses reflect how the situation is presented, not just how long it lasted.

words.means: disparar = to shoot; disparan = they shoot
me despierto = I wake up; te despiertas = you wake up
espero = I hope; esperamos = we hope
pueda = can, subjunctive for he or she; puedas = can, subjunctive for tú

concept.line: To express a hope about another subject, use esperar que plus the subjunctive: Espero que vengas, Espero que el doctor pueda ayudarme. With the same subject, an infinitive is often natural: Espero ver bien. Later, dudo que and necesito que also introduce subjunctive clauses.

words.means: algún = some, before a masculine singular noun

dudo = I doubt; dudar = to doubt

funciona = works; funcionar = to work, to function
se rompe = it breaks; se romperá = it will break
termina = ends; termine = ends, present subjunctive

será = he, she or it will be
acompañarnos = to come with us; acompañar = to accompany
salimos = we leave; salieron = they left
llamamos = we call, including naming something

concept.line: hay introduces something that exists or is available: Hay espacio, Hay dos personas. había presents past background: Había espacio. In this impersonal construction, standard Spanish keeps haber singular even with a plural noun. Use estar to locate a specific person or thing: El señor está aquí.

words.means: cuidarte = to take care of yourself
por mi cuenta = on my own; por tu cuenta = on your own
prueba = piece of evidence; pruebas = evidence
mentir = to lie; mienten = they lie
ganar = to earn; gano = I earn; ganamos = we earn
señalar = to point out; señale = point out, addressing usted

comiendo = eating; comen = they or you all eat
leyendo = reading; lee = he or she reads

concept.line: A form of estar plus a gerund presents an action in progress: Estoy trabajando. The gerund stays the same for every person: estamos comiendo. Spanish also uses the simple present in many situations where English uses an -ing form.

words.means: perder = to lose; perdemos = we lose
gane = wins, subjunctive after a hope
hables = speak, in a negative tú command; hablas = you speak
durmiendo = sleeping; duerma = sleeps, subjunctive; dormía = was sleeping

concept.line: Keep an action in the infinitive after para, antes de, después de and sin: para descansar, antes de salir, después de comer, sin hablar. English often uses -ing after before, after and without. For a purpose involving another subject, use para que plus the subjunctive.

words.means: vender = to sell; vendo = I sell; venderlo = to sell it
buen = good, before a masculine singular noun
llegue = I, he or she arrives, subjunctive; llegues = you arrive, subjunctive
esté = I, he or she is, subjunctive; estemos = we are, subjunctive

concept.line: For an event still ahead, use cuando plus the subjunctive: Cuando llegues, te llamo. English normally uses a present form here too. The time clause can come first or last; a first time clause is followed by a comma. A present habit or completed past event normally uses the indicative.

words.means: recuerdo = I remember; recuerdas = you remember; recordar = to remember

lessons.title: Get a photo the right way up

words.means: al revés = upside down, the wrong way around
salen = they or you all appear
girar = to turn; gira = turn, addressing tú

lessons.title: Get help with a difficult text

words.means: dices = you say; digas = you say, subjunctive

concept.line: que links a person or thing to more information: la parte que quiero leer. donde describes a place: la casa donde vivo. lo que means what or the thing that without a named noun before it: Entiendo lo que dices.

With estar, a posture adjective says how someone is positioned and a gerund says what they are doing: Está acostado leyendo. The adjective agrees with the person; the gerund does not change: sentada leyendo, acostado leyendo.

words.means: seguir = to follow; sigo = I follow
true; that's right in es cierto
habías = you had; habíamos = we had; habían = they or you all had

concept.line: Use imperfect haber plus an unchanged participle for something earlier than a past reference point: Cuando llegué, ella ya había salido. había can mean I, he, she or formal you had; context identifies the subject. Object pronouns go before haber.

words.means: cariño = honey, when addressing someone you love
pude = I was able to; pudimos = we were able to; podía = could, for past background
tuve que = I had to, for a bounded past event

concept.line: pude and tuve que present ability or necessity as a bounded past event: No pude dormir; Tuve que trabajar. podía and tenía que describe past ability, obligation, or ongoing circumstances as background. The choice reflects how you present the situation; an imperfect is not automatically wrong where a preterite is possible.

words.means: escrito, escrita, escritos = written, agreeing in a passive
venden = they sell; vende = he or she sells
prepara = prepares; se prepara = is prepared
leen = they read; se leen = are read

concept.line: ser plus an agreeing participle presents an action: El libro fue escrito por mi hermana. por names the writer. Everyday passive se also focuses on what is done: Se venden casas. Its verb agrees with the things sold: se vende una casa, se venden casas. estar plus a participle instead describes a state.

lessons.title: A film that stays with you

concept.line: Use más ... que for more ... than, menos ... que for less ... than, and tan ... como for as ... as. Adjectives agree with the things described: Esta casa es más pequeña que esa. Keep tan unchanged before an adjective.

words.means: golpear = to hit; golpeas = you hit; no golpees = don't hit
dirijo = I lead; dirigir = to lead

concept.line: Impersonal se talks about people in general without naming a subject: Aquí se habla español; ¿Se puede entrar? The verb is third-person singular. A specific human object takes personal a: Aquí se llama a los padres. Unlike passive se, that object does not make the verb plural.

words.means: better; best with the definite article
worse; worst with the definite article

concept.line: mejor and peor mean better and worse. mayor and menor compare age here: Mi hermano es mayor que yo. A relative superlative uses an article plus más or menos and an adjective: la casa más grande del barrio. As adjectives, mejor, peor, mayor, and menor do not change for gender and add -es in the plural. Adverbial mejor and peor stay unchanged.

words.means: odio = I hate; odias = you hate
pelear = to fight; pelean = they fight

lessons.title: What do you think of it?

concept.line: After most prepositions, use mí and ti: para mí, sin ti. With con, use conmigo and contigo. él and ella keep their forms: de él, con ella. The pronoun él keeps its accent and stays separate from de; only the article el contracts to del.

words.means: lamento = I regret; lamentar = to regret
sentirme = to feel, with myself as the experiencer
fue = he or she went, preterite
caramba = darn, expressing surprise or frustration
se me olvidó = I forgot, presented as a lapse

concept.line: se plus me, te, le, nos, or les presents an event with someone affected: Se me cayó el vaso; Se me olvidó llamar. The verb agrees with the thing affected: se me cayó el vaso, se me cayeron las llaves. This often presents an accident or lapse without making the affected person the grammatical subject.

words.means: discutir = to argue; discutimos = we argue; discuten = they argue
llevarla = to take it; llévala = take it; llevándola = taking it

concept.line: Attach an object pronoun to an infinitive or affirmative command: llevarla, llévala. With an ordinary conjugated verb, put it before: la llevo. A progressive allows estoy llevándola or la estoy llevando. With a negative command it also goes before: no la lleves. Keep paired pronouns together: llévasela, se la llevo.

casita = little house, often said affectionately

concept.line: -ito and -ita can suggest smallness, affection or a softer request: un momentito, un cafecito, una casita. These nouns keep their base noun's gender. cafecito uses -cito and need not mean a smaller coffee. Learn natural forms in context; do not add a diminutive to every noun.
